headline: Georgia's Okefenokee Swamp Earns UNESCO World Heritage Status
meta_description: Georgia's Okefenokee Swamp becomes the state's first UNESCO World Heritage Site, joining America's most iconic natural wonders and protecting one of Earth's mo…
summary_short: Georgia's Okefenokee Swamp has earned UNESCO World Heritage status, becoming the state's first site on the prestigious list and joining the Grand Canyon and Yellowstone.
body:
Georgia's Okefenokee Swamp has achieved a landmark milestone: UNESCO World Heritage Site status, making it the state's first-ever entry on the prestigious international list. The designation recognizes what conservation scientists have long understood—that this 403,000-acre wetland represents a globally irreplaceable ecosystem. It now stands alongside America's most celebrated natural wonders: the Grand Canyon, Sequoia, Everglades, and Yellowstone National Parks. The recognition reflects not only the swamp's stunning present-day biodiversity but also decades of deliberate protection effort that began in earnest over a century ago.

The Okefenokee's path to World Heritage status tells a story of recovery and persistence. In 1918, when conservation efforts first took root, the swamp had already lost 1 million cubic meters of timber to logging. The federal government stepped in during 1936, acquiring most of the wetland and establishing it as a National Wildlife Refuge a year later—the most-visited such refuge east of the Mississippi River. The designation as a RAMSAR Wetland of International Importance followed, and in 2023, the National Parks Service formally nominated it for UNESCO recognition.

What makes the Okefenokee exceptional extends far beyond its size. It is the largest lowland freshwater peatland in the subtropical world, supporting at least 856 plant species, 238 bird species, 48 mammals, and 90 reptile and amphibian species. The swamp harbors endangered longleaf pine forests—fewer than 3 percent of which remain anywhere—and an extraordinary diversity of carnivorous plants. Its peat deposits serve as both a carbon storage system and a historical archive of environmental change. A natural cycle of drought and fire occurring roughly every 20 to 30 years maintains the delicate balance that allows this ecosystem to thrive. That ancient rhythm, now protected on the world stage, ensures this American treasure will endure.
quick_facts: 403,000-acre Georgia wetland joins Grand Canyon and Yellowstone on UNESCO list
Okefenokee supports 238 bird species, 856 plants, and 90 reptile and amphibian species
Most-visited National Wildlife Refuge east of the Mississippi River
Less than 3% of endangered longleaf pine forests remain worldwide
Fire and drought cycle every 20-30 years shapes the unique ecosystem
